generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, almost everything you write draws on studies and theories, so citation is constant. You might quote a precise definition of a construct, where the exact wording matters, or paraphrase a study's finding in your own words. Either way, an in-text citation points the reader to the full reference. Psychology usually uses the APA author-date style, so a citation names the author and year, with a page number when you quote.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students want to use the same sentence from a source: 'Memory for studied material is strengthened by repeated retrieval' (Okafor, 2021, p.44).

Tom writes: Okafor (2021) says that memory for studied material is strengthened by repeated retrieval. The wording is almost identical to the original, but there are no quotation marks. It reads as Tom's own phrasing of a borrowed sentence, so it is neither a clean paraphrase nor a quotation. The citation is there, but the move is muddled.

Amara writes: recalling material repeatedly, rather than simply rereading it, strengthens memory for it (Okafor, 2021). The idea is kept, the words are her own, and the source is cited. Where the exact phrasing mattered, she could instead quote it directly: 'memory for studied material is strengthened by repeated retrieval' (Okafor, 2021, p.44).

Both students used the source. Only Amara made a clean choice between paraphrase and quotation, and cited it correctly.
generatedProse.summary: Bringing a psychology source into your writing means choosing quotation or paraphrase, and citing it either way. Quote the exact words, in quotation marks and with a page number, when the precise wording matters, such as a definition. Paraphrase, in your own words, to show you have understood the finding, which markers reward most. Place the citation next to the idea it supports. The next lesson builds the full APA reference that each citation points to.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara give a page number in one citation but not the other?

items.text: A page number is given with the direct quotation, but the paraphrase needs only the author and year.
Page numbers are optional and she added one at random.
The paraphrase needed a page number, but the quotation did not.
Neither citation really needed a page number.

feedback.correct: That's right. A direct quotation carries a page number; a paraphrase cites author and year.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look at which version quoted the exact words, and which restated the finding.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The direct quotation carries a page number so the reader can find the exact words; the paraphrase needs only author and year.
